newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Gas turns to MMC over pricing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Gas turns to MMC over pricing.

text.p: British Gas Plc decided on Thursday to opt for another Monopolies and Mergers Commission inquiry rather than accept regulator Ofgas's price controls for its gas transmission business.
This would be the second MMC enquiry in four years for British Gas, which is planning to split into two separate companies, TransCo and gas supplier British Gas Energy, early in 1997.
It ensures months of continuing uncertainty for hard-pressed shareholders and employees, and further delays in keenly-awaited price cuts for millions of customers.

Ofgas director-general Clare Spottiswoode expressed "disappointment" at the decision to reject her proposals for a one-off cut of 20 percent in the prices that transmission arm TransCo charges to other suppliers.
This would be followed by four years of charges pegged at 6.5 percentage points below inflation. Ofgas believed this would cut 30 pounds ($47) a year from average domestic gas bills.

But British Gas accused Ofgas of pursuing "unjustified and unworkable proposals" that would slash 400 milion pounds a year from its cash flow, put the safety of its sytsem at risk and lead to further job losses.
Chairman Richard Giordano accused Ofgas of a "flawed" aproach to the review, saying British Gas had been refused access to key reports on which Ofgas had based its decisions.
"It is quite an unusual event to have the foundation of these decisions not subjected to scrutiny by those who have to implement them," he told Reuters Financial Television.
Spottiswoode said her plans were "achievable" and "consistent with the approach taken by other regulators."

The consumer watchdog Gas Consumers Council joined in the row, saying "only the MMC can translate the gobbledygook of recent arguments into questions we can all understand. Is it in the public interest that 18 million consumers should forfeit decades of cheaper gas for the sake of short-term value for two million shareholders?"
Shareholders however appeared to be the most immediate victims of the fallout, with their shares dropping six pence in value to 193 by midday.
Expressing confidence in the outcome of the MMC review, Giordano said: "We believe we will get a very careful scrutiny of the whole subject by the MMC, which we have not had so far."

But he warned that if the MMC does not back British Gas "there will be a diminished reward for shareholders, there will be less resource to sustain the system, and I think if we are in any way to achieve the cost targets which Ofgas is setting there will be job losses."

Ofgas had already scaled back its original demands in August, but British Gas insisted these were still too tough. In an interview, deputy chairman Philip Rogerson, who led British Gas's negotiating team, told Reuters that the two sides had made little progress during weeks of meetings.

Rogerson said the talks foundered on a number of key issues, including Ofgas's approach to accounting for asset valuations and depreciation. He said Ofgas's assumptions on operating costs were also "nothing like" adequate.
But he insisted that the MMC inquiry will not affect British Gas's plans to split. ($1=.6388 Pound)
